sentences.label: Lowering the risk
sentences.text: These add up independently, and these lower the risk: through this sum alone, being a woman takes a typical patient's predicted risk from about 12% to below 1%, and compared with no chest pain symptoms typical angina lowers it to below 1%, non-anginal chest pain to about 1% and atypical angina to about 7%, and fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL to about 2%; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily, from about 22% at 118 to about 8% at 175 beats per minute; sex, chest pain type, fasting blood sugar and maximum heart rate also act through the parts below.

sentences.label: Raising the risk
sentences.text: Each extra vessel coloured by fluoroscopy adds about the same, from about 12% at 0 to about 98% at 2 vessels, flattening out near the top because the predicted risk cannot go much higher; higher cholesterol raises it steadily, from about 5% at 193 mg/dL to about 31% at 308 mg/dL, flattening out near the bottom because the predicted risk cannot go much lower; higher resting blood pressure (from about 7% at 110 mm Hg to about 22% at 155 mm Hg) and older age (from about 10% at 42 to about 13% at 66 years) raise it steadily, and a resting ECG other than normal raises it to about 14%.

Through this sum alone, a flat rather than upsloping ST segment raises it to about 76% and a reversible defect on the thallium scan to about 27%; the ST segment and the thallium scan also act through the parts below.

sentences.label: Rare results

parts.name: heart_disease_logit
parts.original_hypothesis: Root hypothesis: an additive composition that is essentially logistic regression plus three one-sided ReLU corrections. Logit z = -0.680 + LINEAR CORE + 0.746*st_depression_gate + 1.730*female_exang_and_gate - 0.918*thalach_cp3_protective_gate, and the prediction is sigmoid(z) (get_formula renders the output as ReLU, but for this binary task the model applies a sigmoid to the output pre-activation). LINEAR CORE = 19 direct input->output edges, dominated by ca (+2.607, number of vessels), sex:0 (-1.573, women lower risk), chol (+0.870), slope:1 (-0.833, upsloping ST protective), cp:1 (-0.785), slope:2 (+0.743), cp:3 (-0.743), fbs:0 (+0.627), trestbps (+0.519), thal:7 (+0.490), thalach (-0.470), sex:1 (+0.390), thal:4 (+0.383), thal:6 (-0.351), cp:4 (+0.312); age, restecg:0, exang:0/1 near zero. cp:2, fbs:1, restecg:1, restecg:2 are unused. Corrections: (a) ischaemia evidence (ST depression, reversible thal defect) adds risk; (b) women with exercise angina lose most of their sex protection (AND gate, +2.07 logit); (c) high max heart rate, especially with non-anginal pain, removes extra risk. Evidence (train, n=242): accuracy 0.876, AUC 0.947. Linear core logit SD 4.90 vs gates 0.78 / 0.56 / 0.49. Linear core alone AUC 0.930; mean-ablating each gate gives AUC 0.938 / 0.940 / 0.945, so together the nonlinear parts add ~+0.017 train AUC. SHAP (probability scale): ca 0.170 >> sex:0 0.080 > slope:1 0.063 > cp:3 0.058 > slope:2 0.053 > thal:7 0.050 > chol 0.038 > thalach 0.034 > oldpeak 0.029. Function preservation of the refactored model 1.8e-15; all leaf closed forms exact up to 3-s.f. display rounding (max 0.027).

It switches on mainly with exercise-induced ST depression (oldpeak), more readily when there is a reversible thal defect (thal:7), is pushed down by a downsloping ST segment (slope:3, which is clinically counter-intuitive; it is rare, 7%, and the direct linear core has no slope:3 term, so this is probably how the network absorbs slope:3 at all), and slightly by normal fasting sugar (fbs:0). It enters the logit with weight +0.746, so it only ever adds risk. parts.original_hypothesis: Hypothesis: a protective high-exercise-capacity gate. Serial chain thal:3 -> 3818 -> 2124. 3818 = ReLU(1.003*thal:3 - 0.192) is a normal-thallium indicator taking only the values 0 (abnormal thal) and 0.702 (normal thal, 56% of patients). 2124 = ReLU(1.338*thalach + 0.763*cp:3 - 0.108*3818 - 0.932) fires when maximum heart rate is high, much more readily with non-anginal chest pain (cp:3): active on 80% of cp:3 patients but 10.5% of others (30.6% overall, max 2.88). It enters the logit with weight -0.918, so it only ever lowers risk, adding a hinge to the direct linear thalach (-0.470) and cp:3 (-0.743) terms. The thal:3 branch only moves the threshold by -0.076 (sensitivity 0.025 vs thalach 0.41, cp:3 0.23) and is nearly inert. Evidence (train, n=242): closed form exact; logit contribution SD 0.49; mean-ablation drops train AUC only 0.947 -> 0.945, the weakest of the three gates.

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

settings.effect_scale: log-odds (output pre-activation) for verification; predicted risk for the typical patient for wording

ann_32.text: This part acts on 116 of 242 training patients (48%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly raises the predicted risk of heart disease from above 99% without this part to above 99% with it (on the training data only).
In the training data, 77 of these 116 patients had heart disease.

A higher ST depression on exercise clearly raises the predicted risk of heart disease, and even more so if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect (in an uneven way for patients with a reversible defect on the thallium scan): for a typical patient, ST depression on exercise going from 0.0 mm to 2.8 mm moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 27% to about 76% if the thallium scan shows a reversible defect, and from about 12% to about 32% if thallium stress test result is something other than a reversible defect on the thallium scan.

Other effects: ST depression on exercise past about 1.2 mm raises it in an uneven way; slope of the ST segment at peak exercise depending on fasting blood sugar raises it; a higher ST depression on exercise raises it in an uneven way; ST depression on exercise depending on slope of the ST segment at peak exercise raises it in an uneven way; ST depression on exercise depending on fasting blood sugar raises it steadily for most patients, but for patients with a downsloping ST segment it has a threshold; fasting blood sugar above 120 mg/dL (rather than fasting blood sugar of 120 mg/dL or less) raises it; a reversible defect on the thallium scan (rather than any other thallium stress test result) raises it (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a downsloping ST segment (rather than any other slope of the ST segment at peak exercise) lowers it (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 17 training patients (a downsloping ST segment).

ann_33.text: This part acts on 19 of 242 training patients (8%); nearly all of them are women and patients whose chest pain is brought on by exercise.

For a typical patient it acts on, it raises the predicted risk of heart disease from about 9% without this part to about 43% with it (on the training data only). The model has little data on this: only 19 training patients (patients the part acts on).
In the training data, 12 of these 19 patients had heart disease.

The model gives a slightly lower predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman than if the patient is a man, and even more so if exercise does not bring on chest pain: for a typical patient, going from male to female moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to below 1% if exercise does not bring on chest pain, and from about 12% to about 2% if exercise brings on chest pain.

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if exercise brings on chest pain (about 43%) than if exercise does not bring on chest pain (about 9%) (on the training data only).

Through this part, for a typical patient this part acts on, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if the patient is a woman (about 43%) than if the patient is a man (about 9%) (on the training data only).

ann_34.text: This part acts on 74 of 242 training patients (31%).
For a typical patient it acts on, it slightly lowers the predicted risk of heart disease from about 1% without this part to below 1% with it.
In the training data, 13 of these 74 patients had heart disease.

The model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result is something other than a normal thallium scan than if the thallium scan is normal, and even more so if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain: for a typical patient, going from a normal thallium scan to thallium stress test result other than a normal thallium scan moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 12% to about 37% if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain, and from about 1% to about 4% if the patient has non-anginal chest pain (on the training data only).

For a typical patient, maximum heart rate going from 118 beats per minute to 175 beats per minute moves the predicted risk of heart disease from about 3% to below 1% if the patient has non-anginal chest pain, and from about 22% to about 8% if chest pain type is something other than non-anginal chest pain (it moves slowly at first, then faster for patients with non-anginal chest pain).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: non-anginal chest pain (rather than any other chest pain type) lowers it; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it with nothing until about 147 beats per minute, then steadily; maximum heart rate past about 174 beats per minute lowers it with nothing until about 174 beats per minute, then steadily; any other thallium stress test result (rather than a normal thallium scan) lowers it (on the training data only). The model has little data on some of these: only 6 training patients (of them, patients already past their fold).

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted risk of heart disease if thallium stress test result coded 4 (meaning not recorded) applies (about 90%) than if the thallium scan is normal (about 12%) (on the training data only). Other effects: a higher serum cholesterol raises it steadily; a reversible defect on the thallium scan (rather than a normal thallium scan) raises it; a higher ST depression on exercise raises it in an uneven way; a reversible defect on the thallium scan (rather than a normal thallium scan) raises it; a higher resting blood pressure raises it steadily; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it steadily; a higher maximum heart rate lowers it slowly at first, then faster; female (rather than male) lowers it; and 11 still smaller effects listed in the evidence table (on the training data only).

Smaller effects, each changing the predicted value only slightly: a higher age raises it steadily; any other resting ECG (rather than a normal resting ECG) raises it; chest pain brought on by exercise (rather than no chest pain on exercise) lowers it (on the training data only).

Through one part of the model, ST depression on exercise only adds to the predicted risk of heart disease once it rises above about 1.2 mm (between 0.2 and 1.2 mm for different patients): for a typical such patient, going from 0.0 mm to 3.5 mm moves it from about 14% to about 51%; across patients the change happens in an uneven way (on the training data only).
